considered.name: ReceivableBuild CashStability Growth
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(recch, at), 1))), MIN(RANK(TREND(WINSOR(RATIO(revt, at), 1), 5)), RANK(NEG(VOL(WINSOR(RATIO(oancf, sale), 1), 5)))))
considered.hypothesis: Firms with receivable build, improving revenue productivity, and stable cash conversion should outperform.
considered.reasoning: This avoids reusing the same gross-margin-floor construction and instead asks whether receivable growth is accompanied by stable cash collection economics. Receivables are more likely to represent productive trade credit when demand is improving and operating cash margins are not volatile.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SupplierCredit CostDiscipline
considered.hypothesis: Firms with supplier-credit growth and improving cost efficiency should outperform.
considered.reasoning: This shifts away from simply tightening the prior supplier-credit cash-quality signal and tests a bargaining-power mechanism. Rising payables are more likely to reflect favorable supplier terms rather than distress when cost of goods sold is falling relative to revenue.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NonCashAccrual MarginSmoothing Risk
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(VOL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), sale), 1), 5))), RANK(SUB(VOL(WINSOR(RATIO(oancf, sale), 1), 5), VOL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), revt), 1), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: Firms with unusually stable noncash current-asset accruals while cash margins are more volatile than gross margins should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This directly addresses the wrong-signed history of low-accrual-variability plus margin durability by treating excessive smoothness as a potential warning sign. If cash conversion is volatile but reported unit economics and noncash accruals look stable, reported performance may be smoothed rather than genuinely durable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DepreciationShock MarginInstability
considered.hypothesis: Firms with industry-unusual acceleration in depreciation add-back burden and unstable gross margins should underperform.
considered.reasoning: This avoids the prior mirror-image low-depreciation cash-mapping construction and focuses on shocks in noncash depreciation support. A rising depreciation burden is most concerning when unit economics are unstable, suggesting cash-flow quality is being supported by accounting add-backs amid deteriorating operating reliability.

critic_notes.rationale: Internally consistent and correctly signed, but it is essentially a mechanical rank product of two well-documented effects (Sloan accruals and earnings-volatility/smoothness), so it is a marginally novel packaging rather than a new mechanism.

The 0/1 indicator gate collapses roughly half the cross-section to an exact zero tie, so the short leg mixes high- and low-accrual firms and the portfolio spread no longer tests the stated hypothesis.
This is a near sign-flipped duplicate of the LowAccrual StableROA Interaction proposal in the same batch and adds no incremental economic content.

The denominator (|accruals| + earnings vol) approaches zero for smooth, low-accrual firms, so the raw ratio explodes and the cross-sectional ranking will be driven by division-instability outliers rather than by cash profitability.

Coherent in spirit but the ROE leg uses ceq, which flips sign for negative-book-equity firms and makes the mean-minus-volatility difference uninterpretable, and the overall construct largely restates accruals × profitability-quality already covered by proposal 1.

The pairing of a working-capital accrual component with gross-margin stability is a genuinely distinct conditioning channel (operating-economics durability rather than earnings smoothness), the expression matches the hypothesis, and the expected sign is correct.

This is essentially a mechanical double-sort of two canonical published anomalies (Sloan working-capital accruals and Novy-Marx gross profitability) and is conceptually very close to the archived WorkingCapital-Accrual/Margin composite, so it offers little incremental insight even though the expression and sign are internally coherent.

The conditional logic is internally consistent and economically sensible (receivables build is only alarming when cash conversion is weak), but the oancf/sale leg is close to Ball et al.'s cash-based operating profitability and may dominate the interaction, so the test should include a horse race against that leg alone.

A genuinely conditional refinement rather than a rediscovery — inventory growth is known, but sharpening it on deteriorating gross margin is a defensible markdown/demand-softness mechanism — with sign and expression correctly aligned, though the 3-period TREND is short and invch coverage should be checked.

The two accrual legs in the SUMRANK are highly collinear so the blend adds little, and RE/AT trend is largely a restatement of retained profitability, making this a third near-duplicate of the accruals-times-profitability composite already covered by the archive and Proposal 1.

The quality leg (high mean ROA plus low ROA volatility measured over only three observations) is both a known profitability/earnings-stability anomaly and statistically fragile at that window length, so the modestly novel tax-accrual-noise idea is likely swamped by a noisy, already-published component with weak txach coverage.

The opacity-times-leverage mechanism is the most original proposal here and the sign matches the expression, but the leverage leg has a historically ambiguous (often positively-priced-then-reversed) return relation and the absolute-value accrual measures depend on sparsely populated cash-flow items, so coverage and leg-level diagnostics are essential.

The first leg is verbatim Sloan (1996) balance-sheet accruals (ΔCA − ΔCash − (ΔCL − ΔSTD − ΔTXP) − Dep)/AT, a canonical published anomaly, and the second leg (revenue-intensity trend plus low revenue-intensity volatility) duplicates the conditioner already tested and rejected in "AccrualRelease StableDemand," so the MIN-bottleneck wrapper is the only genuinely new element.

Internally inconsistent under standard Compustat conventions, where RECCH is "decrease (increase) in receivables" so high RATIO(recch, at) means receivables are *falling*, contradicting the stated "rising receivable accruals" and inverting the expected sign — the same sign trap that likely killed the archive's ReceivableAccrual CashMargin Trap.

The mechanism (cash-margin improvement financed by stretching suppliers rather than operating quality) is coherent, sign-consistent with APALCH's increase convention, and substantively different from the archive's payables/level-margin composite, though coverage will be thin and the ACCEL term on a noisy quarterly-to-annual ratio may be mostly noise.

Suffers the same INVCH sign-convention inversion (positive INVCH = inventory decrease) as the receivables proposal, and the economic story — that low margin volatility becomes a *negative* signal conditional on inventory accruals — is asserted rather than argued and is hard to distinguish from the failed gen-0 margin-stability composite.

The persistence leg reproduces the exact SUMRANK(MA(·,5), NEG(VOL(·,5))) construction of the already-rejected TaxPayable StableCashMargin (and is itself the known ROA-level plus earnings-volatility anomaly pair), while |DPC − DP| is largely a reporting/data-alignment artifact rather than an economically interpretable accrual distortion, making this a cosmetic swap of the interaction term.

Replacing the leverage conditioner from OpaqueAccrual LeveragePressure with a retained-earnings-erosion trend is a substantive, economically motivated change (opacity matters most when the cumulative profit base is shrinking) and the expression is sign-consistent, though the RE/AT trend leg overlaps with well-documented distress/RE-based predictors and coverage remains low.

Expression and expected sign are internally consistent and the revenue-minus-cash trend divergence leg is a genuinely different conditioner from the archived receivables signals, though the stated "sign-convention correction" is not actually new (the archived ReceivablesBuild SalesDeceleration Trap already used NEG(recch)) and the divergence leg is close in spirit to a plain accruals proxy.

This is a near-cosmetic variant of the archived InventoryBuild CashMargin Erosion, swapping TREND for MA of the identical oancf/sale ratio, and the resulting construct is essentially the intersection of two published anomalies (inventory growth and cash-based operating profitability) rather than a new mechanism.

The expression cleanly implements the stated smoothing mechanism (high working-capital accruals plus cash-flow volatility exceeding earnings volatility), both legs are consistently scaled by assets so the volatility difference is meaningful, and the negative sign is consistent with the smoothness/cost-of-capital literature without directly replicating a standard tradable anomaly.

Sign conventions and hypothesis are consistent (positive apalch = payables build, NEG trend = margin erosion) and the payables×gross-margin-trend pairing is not in the archive, though it is conceptually adjacent to the already-tested InventoryBuild MarginDeterioration and PayablesFinanced CashFlow Spike and the margin-trend leg is close to change-in-gross-profitability.

The quality leg subtracts an absolute trend gap from a raw trend level without separately ranking or normalizing the two components, so the composite's effective weighting is arbitrary and the signal largely re-treads the archived WorkingCapital Clean DebtCoverage construction with added ad hoc complexity rather than a distinct economic mechanism.

This is the mirrored restatement of the archived DepreciationAdjusted CashDurability signal (both legs negated and the expected sign flipped), expressing the identical economic hypothesis that already tested null, so it offers no substantive new information.

This is a cosmetic re-parameterization of the archived "WorkingCapital ShortDebt Funding Pressure" signal (MUL→MIN, oancf/at→oancf/sale) with identical legs and mechanism, so it tests no new economic idea and merely re-shuffles an already-evaluated result.

Sign conventions and internal logic are coherent, but it is the archived "InventoryBuild CashMargin Erosion" signal with one extra short-debt-trend term bolted into a SUMRANK — an incremental splice of two prior legs rather than a substantively different mechanism, and the added term dilutes the leg that actually produced the -2.89 alpha.

The receivables-build leg is correctly signed and the conditioner (cash-conversion instability plus rising short-term debt reliance) is a genuinely different quality dimension from the previously tested sales-deceleration and revenue-vs-cash-trend versions, though the volatility leg partly recycles the known cash-flow-volatility anomaly.

Both legs are taken verbatim from archived signals (ABS(aoloch/at) and the VOL(oancf)−VOL(ni) smoothing gap), each of which already produced positive alphas directly opposite the hypothesized negative sign, so this recombination has a low prior and adds no new information.

The second leg (trend in ni/at minus trend in oancf/at) is a repackaging of the well-known accrual anomaly and is mechanically correlated with the tax-payable accrual leg, so the "interaction" largely double-counts one published effect rather than crossing distinct themes.

"Low working-capital accrual × durable cash margin" has now been tested three times in the archive (MA, TREND, and MIN-composite variants) and consistently delivered negative alphas against the positive expected sign; swapping MA for TS_MIN is a cosmetic variant that does not diagnose why the pattern keeps inverting.

This is a near-cosmetic variant of the archived "WorkingCapital ShortDebt Funding Pressure," swapping TREND(dlc/lt) for TREND(lct/lt) — two highly collinear measures of liability maturity shift — on an identical wcap-accrual leg, so it is unlikely to constitute new information.

The sign convention on recch/invch is handled correctly, but the signal is essentially the archived "WorkingCapital UnproductiveDemand Build" with DELTA(wcap) decomposed into its receivable/inventory components against the identical NEG(TREND(revt/at)) leg, and both component legs have already failed separately in the archive.

This is the fifth inventory-build interaction in the archive and its only new element is changing the turnover denominator from at to act, a mechanically near-collinear substitution that does not address why the earlier inventory-build variants were uniformly null.

The construction coherently diagnoses why prior clean-accrual/high-cash-margin signals inverted by conditioning the cash-margin spike on receivable liquidation and weakening demand, though retaining EXPECTED_SIGN=negative sits uneasily with the archived predecessor's positive fmb_tstat.

This is a mechanical recombination of two archived signals' legs — the txp-delta leg from "TaxPayable CashCoverage Pressure" and the gross-margin-trend leg from "PayablesStretch MarginErosion" — with no new economic mechanism, and both parents were statistically null.

Flipping the depreciation-burden leg to positive and pairing it with deteriorating asset turnover is an internally consistent "aging, underutilized asset base" story that is not a direct rediscovery, though dpc/at is heavily industry/capital-intensity driven and the signal risks proxying for known capital-intensity and asset-growth effects.

This is effectively the mirror image of the archived "WorkingCapital Clean DebtCoverage" (and cousin of "TaxPayable CashCoverage Pressure"), swapping the trend of oancf/lt for its level and adding a TS_RANK wrapper — a cosmetic reparameterization of an already-tested wcap-accrual × cash-coverage interaction rather than a new mechanism.

The signal is internally consistent (spike × decelerating margin → high value → predicted underperformance) and the ACCEL-based inflection plus own-history TS_RANK is a genuinely different construction from the archived level/trend/volatility margin pairings, though it remains inside a family that has repeatedly failed to deliver aligned FMB and alpha evidence.

This is a one-leg substitution on the archived "ReceivableHarvest CashSpike Trap" (same recch leg, same NEG-TREND revt/at leg, cash-spike swapped for earnings smoothness), and the new leg bets against the well-documented low-earnings-volatility premium without arguing why the conditioning should reverse it.

The industry z-score on depreciation burden is a real methodological addition that addresses the sector-proxy problem in the archived depreciation signals, but the second leg is close to a straight inverted cash-based operating profitability sort (a known published anomaly), so much of any resulting spread may be a rediscovery rather than the interaction.

This is a single-input variant of the archived "TaxPayable Volatility StableSales" (revenue volatility replaced by earnings volatility) and its smooth-earnings leg points the composite toward shorting exactly the low-earnings-volatility firms that the published literature finds earn higher returns.

Decomposing the working-capital leg into the two cash-source components (payables build and receivable collection) with consistent cash-flow sign conventions is a substantive refinement of the archived "WorkingCapital UnproductiveDemand Build," which had a correct-signed FMB slope but essentially zero alpha, so this directly targets the diagnosed weakness rather than restating it.

This is a cosmetic re-parameterization of the archived "WorkingCapital ShortDebt Funding Pressure" signal (same accrual leg plus the same dlc/lt-versus-oancf trend contrast, only re-scaled by lt, industry-demeaned, and differenced instead of SUMRANK'd), so it is unlikely to deliver economically new information.

The construction correctly strips the Compustat working-capital cash-flow lines (recch, invch, apalch) out of oancf and is internally consistent with the positive expected sign, and it offers a genuine diagnosis of why prior low-accrual/high-cash-margin composites inverted — though reviewers should note the first leg is close in spirit to Ball et al.'s published cash-based operating profitability, so the incremental content rests on the accrual-stability interaction.

This merely swaps components between two archived signals ("PayablesStretch RetainedEarningsErosion" / "OtherAccrual RetainedEarningsErosion" and the repeatedly tested DELTA(wcap)/at accrual leg), with re/lt rather than re/at as the only genuinely new element, so it is an incremental recombination rather than a new mechanism.

The sign convention is handled consistently (NEG(recch) = receivable build) and the "productive trade credit" framing is an economically substantive reversal of the archive's uniformly bearish receivable-build priors, but the two conditioning legs are simple fundamental-trend momentum terms that may dominate the accrual leg and are close to already-tested recch×trend combinations.

This is the archived "InventoryBuild CashMargin Erosion" signal with the inventory leg replaced by a 5-period TS_RANK of the identical ratio — a mechanical variant, not the substantively different construction the objective calls for.

It is the archived "DepreciationBurden SalesProductivity Decay" expression with an IND_ZSCORE wrapper borrowed from the archived "IndustryDepreciation CashWeakness" — a direct rediscovery contributing no new economic content.

The expression is internally consistent, but it is essentially a re-pairing of two legs already tested in the archive (DELTA(wcap)/at accruals and the MA pre-working-capital cash margin from "PreWorkingCapital CashDurability"), amounting to Sloan accruals × cash-based operating profitability with the added problem that the balance-sheet WC change and the CF-statement WC strip-out are near-mechanically complementary.

The first leg — the trend difference between reported and working-capital-stripped cash margin, which cleanly isolates the WC contribution to cash-flow improvement — is a genuinely new and well-specified construct with a coherent negative sign, though it is paired with a revenue-productivity-fade leg that has repeatedly failed across the archive and may again dominate the portfolio sort.

Both legs mechanically embed −recch (the quality leg subtracts recch from oancf), so the product partly squares the receivable term rather than forming a true conditional interaction, and the construct is otherwise a recombination of the already-tested "ProductiveTradeCredit Quality" and "PreWorkingCapital CashDurability" legs.

This is a cosmetic variant of the archived "TaxPayable CashCoverage Pressure" (identical tax-payable leg, with oancf/lt coverage swapped for sale/lct), which produced a null fmb_tstat and negligible alpha, and no economic argument is offered for why the denominator change should matter.

Deliberately stripping apalch out of the cash-margin quality leg is the correct fix for the mechanical inflation that plagued the earlier payables signals, and flipping to a positive sign is a substantive rather than cosmetic departure from the several failed "payables stretch is bad" variants — though the induced negative mechanical correlation between the two legs should be checked.

This simply swaps the second leg of the archived "IndustryDepreciation MarginDecay" for the retained-earnings-trend leg already used in two other archive signals, so it is a recombination of tested components with no new mechanism, and the re/at trend leg is largely a proxy for the well-known profitability/distress effect.

This is a cosmetic respecification of the archived "ReceivableBuild MarginFloor Quality" (same NEG(recch) leg, same TS_MIN gross-margin floor), merely swapping the revenue-stability gate for an IND_ZSCORE wrapper, so it cannot deliver evidence that is substantively independent of the prior test.

Economically coherent and correctly signed, but it is the archived "SupplierCredit UnderlyingCashQuality" with one extra MIN gate bolted on — an incremental tightening of an already weak (ls_talpha 1.57) signal that will mainly shrink coverage rather than test a new mechanism.

The Δ(noncash current assets) leg is essentially the classic Sloan working-capital accrual, but replacing the archived margin-acceleration gate with a within-firm margin-trough percentile is a genuinely different conditioning variable and the expression direction matches the stated negative sign.

This is the generation-0 "WorkingCapital Accrual Margin Stability" mechanism (low accrual variability × stable/strong gross margin) re-expressed with a different accrual proxy and TS_MIN instead of VOL, and that ancestor already produced a strongly wrong-signed alpha (ls_talpha −2.28), which the proposal neither acknowledges nor addresses.

The cash-margin-minus-gross-margin percentile divergence is a defensibly new construct for measuring unsupported cash performance and the sign convention is internally consistent, though it sits in a heavily mined "working-capital harvest × cash spike" family where four prior variants were all statistically inconclusive.

This is a mechanical double sign-flip of the archived "DepreciationBurden EarningsCashGap" (both legs negated, expected sign reversed), so it re-tests a null result under a near-monotone transformation rather than proposing a new mechanism, and "low dpc/sale" is largely a capital-intensity proxy already spanned by known investment/asset-growth anomalies.
